The handle calculation has produced a pair in \(S^1\times S^2\) that cannot fit in any three-ball. Both original penultimate cuts fail the positive-scalar-curvature test, but a specified framed slide still reduces the pair. On the metric side, the selected minimizing disk supplies charge on both sides. I’m checking what that charge forces at a finite width, alongside an explicit deformation whose two connector costs can be measured separately.

The cyclic-cover argument now gives a sharp count. For a band winding \(n\) times, the minimum intersection with a nonseparating sphere that misses the stationary knot is \(2n\), yet the same two slides reduce every member of the family without stabilization. The metric calculation also produced a fixed-width example in which each isolated connector crosses \(8\pi^2\) while the joined path stays below \(\pi^2/1000\). I’m checking the manuscript statements against the derivations and rebuilding the reading copies.

I found a further construction that works on the selected minimizing disk itself. It moves the marked disk into a flattened ball and keeps the joined energy below the wall. The price is explicit: its original charge moves into the exterior, including any protected-core charge. I’m checking the two isolated connector costs to determine exactly what this construction proves on that source.

**The original charged disk now admits an exact round-product face with both capped sides Yamabe-positive.** On any fixed smooth positive subcritical source of energy \(e_i\), the joined path can stay below \(e_i+\eta<8\pi^2\) for arbitrarily small \(\eta>0\). The cost is explicit. In each chirality the disk ends with zero charge, and its original charge \(m_i^\pm\) reappears in the outer collar, up to an error of at most \(\eta\). Both isolated connectors can exceed \(8\pi^2\) at the same native width. For a matched path that retains core charges \(q_i^\pm\), the joined peak must instead reach at least \(I^+(M)+\max(q_i^+,q_i^-)\).
